title: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition) · Units 09–10
description: Curated B2 idioms for describing people, relationships, social-media vocabulary, attraction, disagreements, dating and reconciliation.
sourceNotice: Prepared from the user-supplied book for personal study. Vocabulary selections reflect teaching topics and exercises; all example sentences and usage notes were independently written, without reproducing exercise passages or illustrations.

audit.scope: Units 09–10 teaching pages, idiom tables and illustrations, -mate forms, relationship verb tables, exercises and matching answer-key sections checked for core vocabulary and contextual distinctions.
audit.pronunciation: Conservative British English phonemic IPA is supplied for confident standalone words and a few short expressions; longer idioms generally omit IPA to avoid unsupported connected-speech guesses.
audit.languagePolicy: All content is English except Brazilian Portuguese translations in pt.
audit.reviewMethod: Source and answer-key extraction and comparison; editorial checks for idiom wording, register, usage and original examples; structural schema, stable IDs, content origin, IPA formatting and conservative word/sentence TTS checks. No application-browser tests were performed.
audit.limitations: No bundled audio tracks. Live VocabLab import, browser TTS and speech-recognition behaviour were not tested.

units.title: Unit 09 — Idioms describing people
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 24–25 (PDF pages 25–26).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: People: idioms, personality and social judgement
learningObjectives: Describe very kind, unkind and irritating people using idioms with gold, heart, nails and nerves.
Understand idioms built around head, including memory, calculation, sensible behaviour and avoiding problems.
Recognise informal expressions for eccentric, exaggerated and moderate behaviour.
Apply classroom-related character labels while recognising when they sound insulting or teasing.
Keep key articles, possessives and prepositions in idiomatic expressions accurate.

sectionsChecked: C: How people relate to the social norm
D: Who’s who in the class?

items.pt: ter um coração de ouro; ser muito bondoso
items.example: Despite her busy schedule, she has a heart of gold and always helps her neighbours.
items.note: Very positive idiom for someone kind and generous; change have to has/had to match the subject.

items.example: Our former manager was as hard as nails when staff needed support.
items.note: Describes someone tough and unsympathetic, especially to other people's difficulties.

items.example: The children were as good as gold throughout the long train journey.
items.note: Usually describes a child or children who behave exceptionally well; not necessarily moral goodness.

items.pt: uma pessoa muito desagradável; sujeito detestável
items.example: He seemed friendly at first, but he turned out to be a nasty piece of work.
items.note: Strongly insulting idiom for an unpleasant or cruel person; use with care.

items.word: have your heart in the right place
items.pt: ter boas intenções; ter bom coração
items.example: Her advice was clumsy, but she had her heart in the right place.
items.note: Someone means well and is kind even if their actions seem misguided or awkward; change your to suit the subject.

items.example: The new landlord is an awkward customer when it comes to repairs.
items.note: Informal expression for a difficult person; customer does not have to be buying anything.

items.pt: uma pessoa irritante; um pé no saco
items.example: That neighbour is a pain in the neck because he complains about everything.
items.note: Informal idiom for someone or something annoying; the fixed form uses in the neck.

items.pt: me irritar; me dar nos nervos
items.example: Constant interruptions really get on my nerves when I am concentrating.
items.note: Change my to your, his, her, our, etc.; do not say get on the nerves in the usual expression.

items.pt: ter a cabeça no lugar; ser sensato
items.example: I trust Nadia with difficult decisions because she has her head screwed on.
items.note: Informal: think sensibly and make sound decisions; your changes with the person described.

items.pt: não sofrer de vertigem em locais altos; lidar bem com altura
items.example: You need a head for heights to work safely on that exposed platform.
items.note: Means feeling comfortable at height without vertigo; not the same as being tall or simply enjoying tall buildings.

items.word: have a head like a sieve
items.pt: ter memória de peixe; ser muito esquecido
items.example: I have a head like a sieve, so I write every appointment in my calendar.
items.note: Informal idiom for a very bad memory; compare have a good head for figures.

items.word: have a good head for figures
items.pt: ser bom com números; ter facilidade com cálculos
items.example: Ask Mei to check the budget; she has a good head for figures.
items.note: Figures means numerical information, calculations or accounts; not pictures or body shape.

items.word: have your head in the clouds
items.pt: viver no mundo da lua; ser desligado da realidade
items.example: He has his head in the clouds if he thinks the business can launch without funding.
items.note: Means having unrealistic thoughts or plans; your changes with the subject.

items.pt: ser muito superior a; estar muito à frente de
items.example: Her presentation was head and shoulders above the others in clarity and detail.
items.note: Comparative idiom normally used with be and followed by the person or things being compared with.

items.word: bury your head in the sand
items.pt: fazer vista grossa; fingir que o problema não existe
items.example: We cannot bury our heads in the sand about the security risks.
items.note: Refusing to face an unpleasant fact or problem; possessive and head may change with the subject.

items.pt: manter a calma; não perder a cabeça
items.example: She managed to keep her head while everyone else was panicking.
items.note: Remain calm and think clearly during pressure or danger; opposite of lose your head.

items.pt: uma pessoa excêntrica; uma figura estranha
items.example: People thought the inventor was an odd-ball until her idea succeeded.
items.note: Informal noun for an unusual or eccentric person; also commonly spelled oddball, without a hyphen.

items.example: His reaction to a minor disagreement was completely over the top.
items.note: Informal: excessive or more dramatic than the situation deserves; often abbreviated OTT in British English.

items.example: I'd go round the bend if I had to hear that alarm all day.
items.note: Very informal exaggeration meaning become extremely frustrated or behave irrationally; avoid using casually about a real mental-health condition.

items.example: Her political views are fairly middle-of-the-road.
items.note: Neither radical nor strongly on either side, particularly in politics or opinions; can also mean unadventurous.

items.pt: o queridinho do professor; a queridinha da professora
items.section: D · Classroom and everyday character idioms
items.example: The other pupils teased him for being the teacher's pet.
items.note: Usually a mildly negative label for a teacher's favourite student; use the teacher's pet.

items.pt: o melhor da turma; primeiro da classe
items.section: D · Classroom and everyday character idioms
items.example: After months of hard work, she finished top of the class.
items.note: Describes the student with the highest marks or academic performance.

items.section: D · Classroom and everyday character idioms
items.example: He can sound like a know-all when he corrects everyone at meetings.
items.note: British informal disapproving noun for someone who behaves as if they know everything.

items.section: D · Classroom and everyday character idioms
items.example: Don't be such a big-head just because you won one prize.
items.note: Informal disapproving label for a person with an exaggerated opinion of their own ability or importance.

items.section: D · Classroom and everyday character idioms
items.example: Come on, lazy-bones, we've got a lot to do this morning!
items.note: Informal often teasing noun for a lazy person; normally used with a or as direct address.

items.example: Their bone-idle flatmate never helps with the cleaning.
items.note: Very informal British adjective meaning extremely lazy; mentioned as an alternative in the answer key to Exercise 9.2.

units.title: Unit 10 — Relationships
units.source: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition); printed pages 26–27 (PDF pages 27–28).
units.bookTitle: English Vocabulary in Use — Upper-intermediate (4th Edition)
units.category: People: friendship, social media and relationships
learningObjectives: Distinguish degrees of friendship and acquaintanceship and recognise common -mate compounds.
Use romantic and family relationship vocabulary with correct grammar and register.
Describe online connections, messages, comments, tagging and unfriending.
Express liking, admiration, attraction, dislike and contempt at different strengths.
Use relationship and dating phrasal verbs in realistic contexts and avoid make friends and affair errors.

sectionsChecked: C: Liking and not liking someone
D: Phrases and idioms for relationships and dating

items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: Sofia has been my best friend since primary school.
items.note: A particularly close friend; not interchangeable with a casual acquaintance.

items.pt: bom amigo; boa amiga; amigo próximo
items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: I asked a good friend for advice about changing jobs.
items.note: Means a genuine friend, though not necessarily one's single closest friend.

items.pt: conhecido; conhecida com quem se tem pouco contato
items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: She's only a casual acquaintance from the gym.
items.note: Someone you know slightly rather than a close personal friend; acquaintance is a person, not an intimate friendship.

items.pt: pessoa com quem se divide uma casa
items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: My housemate cooks dinner on Tuesdays, and I cook on Thursdays.
items.note: Someone sharing the same house; not necessarily a close friend or a romantic partner.

items.pt: pessoa com quem se divide um apartamento
items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: My flatmate and I split the electricity bill.
items.note: British English; someone sharing a flat. American English often uses roommate more broadly.

items.pt: pessoa com quem se divide um quarto; colega de quarto
items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: My roommate at university liked to study late at night.
items.note: Traditionally a person sharing a room; in American English also commonly used for a person sharing a home.

items.pt: colega de classe; colega de turma
items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: I recognised an old classmate at the conference.
items.note: Person who is or was in the same class, not necessarily a friend.

items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: A workmate offered to cover my shift.
items.note: Informal and common in manual or non-professional settings; colleague is often more neutral or professional.

items.pt: colega de trabalho; colega de profissão
items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: I discussed the results with a colleague from another laboratory.
items.note: Someone you work with, usually in a professional context; often more formal than workmate.

items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: My ex and I are still on friendly terms.
items.note: Informal noun for a former romantic partner; also used as a prefix in ex-husband and ex-girlfriend.

items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: His ex-girlfriend now lives in a different city.
items.note: Ex- indicates a previous relationship; it does not itself say whether contact continues.

items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: She shares childcare arrangements with her ex-husband.
items.note: A man previously married to someone; use ex-wife for a former wife.

items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: They've been in a steady relationship for nearly three years.
items.note: A stable continuing romantic relationship rather than a casual or short-lived one.

items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: Her partner came with her to the graduation ceremony.
items.note: Can be a romantic partner or a business partner; relationship status is not necessarily married.

items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: They've been married for ten years.
items.note: We say be married to someone; not married with someone.

items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: My parents-in-law are visiting us at the weekend.
items.note: Plural for a spouse's parents; compare mother-in-law and father-in-law.

items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: My mother-in-law taught me how to make that dish.
items.note: Plural is mothers-in-law, not mother-in-laws.

items.section: A · Types of relationship and closeness
items.example: Her father-in-law offered to help with the move.
items.note: Plural is fathers-in-law, not father-in-laws.

items.pt: entrar em uma rede social; cadastrar-se em uma rede social
items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: She joined a social network to reconnect with old classmates.
items.note: Join a network or community; join normally takes a direct object, not join to.

items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: You can acquire hundreds of online friends without knowing them personally.
items.note: The unit uses acquire friends for accumulating social-network connections; for real-life friendships, make friends is normally more natural.

items.pt: ampliar a rede de contatos; aumentar os contatos
items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: Over several years, he built up his contacts in the industry.
items.note: Build up means gradually increase; your changes according to the subject.

items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: She has a contact who works at the publishing company.
items.note: A person you can reach or know through social or professional networks.

items.word: invite someone to become your friend
items.pt: convidar alguém para ser seu amigo numa rede social
items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: He invited me to become his friend on the platform.
items.note: Online invitation to establish a social-media connection; offline English more often uses make friends with someone.

items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: She refused to accept a friend request from an unfamiliar account.
items.note: Common modern online collocation for approving someone as a social-media friend; it expands on the book’s use of accept online friends.

items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: Students can interact with friends through group chats.
items.note: Interact with someone, not interact someone; can involve messages, reactions or comments.

items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: We exchanged messages before agreeing on a time to meet.
items.note: Exchange something with someone; implies communication in both directions.

items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: Please think carefully before you post comments about colleagues online.
items.note: Post means publish content to a website or social media; also post a photo or update.

items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: I only share photos with people I know well.
items.note: Common combination: share photos with someone.

items.pt: marcar seus amigos em fotos ou publicações
items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: Ask permission before you tag your friends in a public photo.
items.note: On social media, tag someone in a photo or post means identify them by name or account.

items.pt: desfazer amizade com alguém numa rede social
items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: She decided to unfriend someone who kept sending abusive messages.
items.note: Remove someone from a social-network friends list, rather than necessarily ending an offline friendship.

items.pt: excluir alguém da lista de amigos numa rede social
items.section: B · Online relationships and social networking
items.example: After the argument, he defriended the person on the platform.
items.note: Variant of unfriend in the unit; unfriend is more widespread today.

items.example: I like my new supervisor because she listens to the whole team.
items.note: Basic verb of positive feeling; compare love and adore for stronger feeling.

items.example: She loves her grandparents and calls them every Sunday.
items.note: Strong positive affection; may refer to family, friends or a romantic partner.

items.pt: adorar alguém; gostar muito de alguém
items.example: The children adore their music teacher.
items.note: Strong affection or admiration; can be less exclusively romantic than love.

items.example: He used to idolise the footballer when he was younger.
items.note: British spelling; American English idolize. Means admire someone intensely, sometimes uncritically.

items.example: I dislike his behaviour, but I don't dislike him as a person.
items.note: More neutral and often weaker than can't stand or loathe.

items.example: I can't stand people who interrupt whenever someone else speaks.
items.note: Strong informal dislike; can also be followed by a noun or -ing verb.

items.pt: detestar alguém; ter aversão a alguém
items.example: She loathes anyone who deliberately mistreats animals.
items.note: Very strong dislike; the final th is voiced /ð/, unlike in loath /ləʊθ/.

items.example: I respect my manager because she admits her mistakes.
items.note: Can respect a person without liking them personally.

items.pt: admirar alguém; ter alguém como exemplo
items.example: Younger researchers look up to her because of her integrity.
items.note: Phrasal verb: admire and respect someone; opposite of look down on.

items.example: He admires his sister's determination.
items.note: Admire a person or a quality they possess; often for achievements or character.

items.pt: menosprezar alguém; olhar alguém de cima para baixo
items.example: It is unfair to look down on someone because of their occupation.
items.note: Treat someone as inferior; opposite in meaning to look up to.

items.example: He despises leaders who abuse their power.
items.note: Very strong contempt or dislike, often involving lack of respect.

items.pt: atrair alguém; despertar atração em alguém
items.example: Her sense of humour attracted him immediately.
items.note: Attract can mean draw romantic interest, attention or other things depending on context.

items.example: She was attracted to him but wasn't ready for a relationship.
items.note: Fixed preposition: attracted to, not attracted for.

items.pt: estar a fim de alguém; sentir atração por alguém
items.example: I think Mia fancies her new colleague.
items.note: Informal British English for finding someone romantically or sexually attractive; not the same as admire.

items.pt: não despertar interesse em alguém; não mexer com alguém
items.example: Everyone praised the actor, but his performance left me cold.
items.note: Someone or something fails to interest or excite you, including in romantic attraction.

items.pt: não me atrair; não me despertar interesse
items.example: That kind of music just doesn't do anything for me.
items.note: Informal equivalent of leave me cold; me can change with the person.

items.example: She gets on well with nearly everyone in the department.
items.note: British English; American English often uses get along well with. Requires with when naming the person.

items.example: We don't always see eye to eye on money, but we respect each other.
items.note: Often used in the negative: not see eye to eye, commonly on or about a topic.

items.pt: brigar com alguém; desentender-se com alguém
items.example: He fell out with his brother over a family decision.
items.note: British informal phrasal verb for quarrelling; past tense fell out, not fell up.

items.pt: ter um caso amoroso; ter um relacionamento extraconjugal
items.example: The novel follows a couple whose marriage suffers when one partner has an affair.
items.note: Usually a secret sexual or romantic relationship involving someone already committed to another partner; use have, not make.

items.example: We argued yesterday, but we made it up this morning.
items.note: Become friendly again after a quarrel; make up with someone is also natural. Here it is not invent a story.

items.pt: namorar alguém; sair com alguém romanticamente
items.example: She's been dating someone from her art class for a few weeks.
items.note: Refers to spending time with a romantic interest; no preposition is needed before the person.

items.pt: sair juntos; estar se conhecendo romanticamente
items.example: They've been seeing each other since the summer.
items.note: In this context means dating; elsewhere the same phrase can simply mean meet or see one another.

items.pt: começar a namorar; ficar juntos como casal
items.example: They got together after working on the same project for a year.
items.note: Romantic sense of beginning a relationship; can also mean meet socially.

items.example: It can take time to make friends in a new country.
items.note: The unit explicitly warns against get friends or find friends for this meaning.

items.example: They had a row about how to share the rent.
items.note: British English for an argument; this noun is pronounced /raʊ/, unlike row /rəʊ/ meaning a line.

items.example: After a brief quarrel, they apologised to each other.
items.note: An angry disagreement; have a quarrel with someone, often about or over something.
